policy.contributing:
# Contributing to sqlite3-ruby

**This document is a work-in-progress.**

This doc is a short introduction on how to modify and maintain the sqlite3-ruby gem.


## Architecture notes

### Decision record

As of 2024-09, we're starting to keep some architecture decisions in the subdirectory `/adr`, so
please look there for additional information.

### Garbage collection

All statements keep pointers back to their respective database connections.
The `@connection` instance variable on the `Statement` handle keeps the database
connection alive.

We use `sqlite3_close_v2` in `Database#close` since v2.1.0 which defers _actually_ closing the
connection and freeing the underlying memory until all open statements are closed; though the
`Database` object will immediately behave as though it's been fully closed. If a Database is not
explicitly closed, it will be closed when it is GCed.

`Statement#close` finalizes the underlying statement. If a Statement is not explicitly closed, it
will be closed/finalized when it is GCed.


## Debugging memory issues

Please install `valgrind` and `gdb` before you use the tools in this section.

Run the test suite under valgrind and [`ruby_memcheck`](https://github.com/Shopify/ruby_memcheck) to
look for memory leaks and other memory errors:

``` sh
bundle exec rake compile test:valgrind
```

If you can't install valgrind on your system, use the `sqlite3-dev` docker image, which contains
valgrind:

``` sh
# build the image
bundle exec rake docker:dev:build

# run the test suite in a container
bundle exec rake docker:dev:test

# run the test suite under valgrind in a container
bundle exec rake docker:dev:test:valgrind
```

Each `docker:dev:test` task builds the image first, then mounts your working copy at `/sqlite3` in
the container. Note that the container compiles into the mounted working copy, so please re-run
`rake compile` on your machine afterwards.

Run the test suite in the debugger:

``` sh
bundle exec rake compile test:gdb
```

You can also run the test suite with a variety of GC behaviors, which is useful to localize some
classes of memory bugs. Set the `SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL` environment variable (see `test/helper.rb`
for more info). A more stressful level finds more bugs, but makes the suite slower:

``` sh
# ordinary GC behavior (the default)
SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL=normal bundle exec rake compile test

# minor GC after each test
SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL=minor bundle exec rake compile test

# major GC after each test
SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL=major bundle exec rake compile test

# major GC after each test, and GC compaction after every 20 tests
SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL=compact bundle exec rake compile test

# verify references after compaction, after every 20 tests
# (see https://alanwu.space/post/check-compaction/)
SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL=verify bundle exec rake compile test

# run each test with GC "stress mode" on
SQLITE3_TEST_GC_LEVEL=stress bundle exec rake compile test
```

The `compact` and `verify` levels fall back to `normal` on a platform that does not support GC
compaction. The `stress` level makes the suite about 150 times slower, and it makes
timing-sensitive tests unreliable.


## Building gems

As a prerequisite please make sure you have `docker` correctly installed, so that you're able to cross-compile the native gems.

Run `bin/build-gems` which will package gems for all supported platforms, and run some basic sanity tests on those packages using `bin/test-gem-set` and `bin/test-gem-file-contents`.


## Updating the version of libsqlite3

Update `/dependencies.yml` to reflect:

- the version of libsqlite3
- the URL from which to download
- the checksum of the file, which will need to be verified manually (see comments in that file)


## Making a release

A quick checklist to cutting a release of the sqlite3 gem:

Prep
- [ ] Make sure CI is green!
- [ ] Update `CHANGELOG.md` and `lib/sqlite3/version.rb`
- [ ] Create a git tag using a format that matches the pattern `v\d+\.\d+\.\d+`, e.g. `v1.3.13`
- [ ] `git push && git push --tags`

Automated build and release
- [ ] Run workflow https://github.com/sparklemotion/sqlite3-ruby/actions/workflows/release.yml
- [ ] Copy checksums from the push job

Manual build and release
- [ ] Run `bin/build-gems` and make sure it completes and all the tests pass
- [ ] `for g in gems/*.gem ; do gem push $g ; done`

Post-release
- [ ] Create a release at https://github.com/sparklemotion/sqlite3-ruby/releases and include sha2 checksums

open.title: Fix Statement#execute parameters persisting into later executions
open.body:
## Motivation

A parameter passed to `Statement#execute` stays bound after that execution, as [@jeremyevans reported in #740](https://github.com/sparklemotion/sqlite3-ruby/discussions/740):

```ruby
stmt = db.prepare "SELECT :a + :b"
stmt.execute(a: 1, b: 2).to_a # => [[3]]
stmt.execute(a: 2).to_a       # => [[4]], b is still 2
stmt.execute.to_a             # => [[4]]
```

[`Statement#execute`](https://github.com/sparklemotion/sqlite3-ruby/blob/90d52d5483090897be2baaa549d7482c2bcd1c7e/lib/sqlite3/statement.rb#L96-L106) binds its arguments with `#bind_params` and never undoes them. Values bound with `#bind_params` before `#execute` must still persist, so `#execute` cannot simply clear every binding:

```ruby
stmt.bind_params(a: 1)
stmt.execute(b: 2).to_a # => [[3]]
stmt.execute(b: 3).to_a # => [[4]]
```

## Details

SQLite has no API to read a bound value, so `Statement#bind_param` and `#bind_params` now record each value in a Hash on the statement, keyed by the parameter index SQLite resolved. An unfrozen String is recorded as a frozen copy made with `String.new` (or `SQLite3::Blob.new`), because SQLite copies its bytes at bind time and the caller may mutate it afterwards. `String.new` runs no subclass hooks, and the copy is made before binding.

`#execute` still binds its arguments through `#bind_params` and `#bind_param`, so subclasses that override them keep working, but those values are not recorded. After such an `#execute`, the next `#execute` or the next value bound by `#bind_param` or `#bind_params` calls `sqlite3_clear_bindings()` and rebinds the recorded values, so placeholders set only by the earlier `#execute` become NULL. `#bind_param` binds the new value before restoring, so a bind that raises on a running statement leaves that statement's bindings alone.

With this change, the first example returns `[[3]]`, `[[nil]]`, `[[nil]]`. A value passed to `#execute` also overrides a `#bind_param` value only for that execution.

Calling `#bind_params` with no values binds nothing and restores nothing. `ResultSet#reset` with no arguments therefore still rewinds with the values passed to `#execute`, as it did before.

`#clear_bindings!` also forgets the recorded values. Its documentation said it reset the statement; it now says it sets every placeholder to NULL.

`#bind_param` and `#clear_bindings!` are now Ruby methods wrapping the C implementations, which are private.

## Additional information

Code that passes a value to `#execute` and expects a later `#execute` to reuse it must now bind that value with `#bind_params`.

The recorded Hash keeps the last value bound to each parameter alive until that parameter is rebound or `#clear_bindings!` is called. A cached statement therefore holds the last values bound with `#bind_param` or `#bind_params`. Except while an `#execute` overrides them, SQLite holds its own copy of the same values. On the path Rails uses (`reset!`, `bind_params`, `to_a` on a cached statement), recording costs one allocation per unfrozen String bound. On a one-row in-memory query binding an Integer and a String, that path takes 1.52 µs per call, against 1.23 µs with the recording removed (best of 4 runs of 500,000 calls).

Resolves #751.

open.title: Ractor support (supersedes #365)
open.body:
Supersedes #365, rebased onto main. The original commits' authors are credited as co-authors.

## What this does

Declares the C extension Ractor-safe when SQLite is built thread-safe, so each Ractor can open and use its **own** connections. Passing a `Database` between Ractors still raises `Ractor::Error` (see `RACTOR.md`).

## Changes beyond #365

- **Statement status symbols filled at Init.** `setup_stmt_stat_symbols` was lazy, and its "already filled?" check only looked at slot 0, so a second Ractor could see a partly filled table. It now runs once in `init_sqlite3_statement`.
- **`define_aggregator` works outside the main Ractor.** The proxy class kept the template and name in class instance variables, which raises `Ractor::IsolationError` in a non-main Ractor. They are now captured in closures (`define_singleton_method`). No API change.
- **`VERSION_INFO` is deeply frozen**, so any Ractor can read it.
- **Dropped the FULLMUTEX "shareable database" part.** SQLite's serialized mode makes the C calls safe, but a `Database` also holds Ruby state (registered functions, aggregators, collations, handlers) that can't be shared between Ractors. Marking it shareable would expose that state.
- **Ractor tests run in a child process with a timeout.** On Ruby 4.0, once a process has started any Ractor, `ObjectSpace.each_object` returns nothing, which broke `test_aggregate_instances_are_released_after_each_query` whenever the Ractor tests ran first. A child process isolates that, and turns a hang into a failure instead of a stalled job. This may account for the hangs seen on #365. I only tested on 4.0.5, so CI will tell for the other Rubies.

## Testing

On Ruby 4.0.5, arm64-darwin:

- The full suite passes with three different seeds (360 runs). Linting is clean on the changed files.
- Reverting the `define_aggregator` or `VERSION_INFO` change makes the matching new test fail.
- A standalone stress script passes with 2, 8, 16 and 32 Ractors. Each Ractor uses its own in-memory connection with every callback type (trace, authorizer, function, aggregator, collation, statement timeout, statement stats), and all Ractors also make contended writes to one shared WAL file.

<details><summary>stress script</summary>

```ruby
# Stress sqlite3 from multiple Ractors. Each Ractor owns its connections;
# nothing but strings and integers crosses a Ractor boundary.
#
#   ruby ractor_stress.rb [ractors=8] [iterations=200]

require "sqlite3"
require "tmpdir"

Warning[:experimental] = false

RACTORS = Integer(ARGV[0] || 8)
ITERS = Integer(ARGV[1] || 200)
dir = Dir.mktmpdir
shared = File.join(dir, "shared.db")

SQLite3::Database.new(shared) do |db|
  db.execute "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL"
  db.execute "CREATE TABLE log (r INTEGER, i INTEGER, note TEXT)"
end

class Summer
  def initialize = @sum = 0
  def step(v) = @sum += v.to_i
  def finalize = @sum
end

class ReverseCollation
  def compare(a, b) = b <=> a
end

def workload(id, iters, shared)
  checks = 0
  iters.times do |i|
    # private in-memory database exercising every callback path
    SQLite3::Database.new(":memory:", results_as_hash: (i.odd?)) do |db|
      traced = 0
      db.trace { |_sql| traced += 1 }
      db.statement_timeout = 10_000
      db.authorizer = ->(*) { true }
      db.create_function("double", 1) { |fn, x| fn.result = x.to_i * 2 }
      db.define_aggregator("summer", Summer.new)
      db.collation("rev", ReverseCollation.new)

      db.execute "CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, s TEXT)"
      db.transaction do
        stmt = db.prepare("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?, ?)")
        50.times { |n| stmt.execute(n, "s#{n}") }
        stmt.close
      end

      sum = db.get_first_value("SELECT summer(double(a)) FROM t")
      raise "aggregate #{sum}" unless sum == 2450

      first = db.get_first_value("SELECT s FROM t ORDER BY s COLLATE rev LIMIT 1")
      raise "collation #{first}" unless first == "s9"

      stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM t WHERE a > ?")
      rows = stmt.execute(10).to_a
      raise "rows #{rows.size}" unless rows.size == 39
      raise "stat" unless stmt.stat(:vm_steps).is_a?(Integer) && stmt.stat.key?(:sorts)
      stmt.close

      begin
        db.execute "SELECT * FROM nope"
        raise "expected SQLException"
      rescue SQLite3::SQLException
      end

      raise "trace" unless traced > 0
      checks += 1
    end

    # shared file database: one connection per Ractor, contended writes
    SQLite3::Database.new(shared) do |db|
      db.busy_timeout = 5000
      db.execute "INSERT INTO log VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [id, i, "r#{id}"]
      db.get_first_value("SELECT count(*) FROM log")
    end
  end
  raise "version_info" unless SQLite3::VERSION_INFO[:gem][:version] == SQLite3::VERSION
  checks
end

t0 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
ractors = RACTORS.times.map do |id|
  Ractor.new(id, ITERS, shared) { |id, iters, shared| workload(id, iters, shared) }
end
results = ractors.map(&:value)
elapsed = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t0

total = SQLite3::Database.new(shared).then { |db| db.get_first_value("SELECT count(*) FROM log").tap { db.close } }
expected = RACTORS * ITERS
puts "ruby #{RUBY_VERSION} sqlite3 #{SQLite3::VERSION} (libsqlite #{SQLite3::SQLITE_LOADED_VERSION})"
puts "#{RACTORS} ractors x #{ITERS} iterations: checks=#{results.sum} log rows=#{total}/#{expected} in #{elapsed.round(2)}s"
exit(results.sum == expected && total == expected ? 0 : 1)
```

</details>

## A related observation (not addressed here)

If the main Ractor exits while worker Ractors are still in the middle of queries, the process can hang during exit. Ruby's exit-time finalizer frees a leftover `Statement`, and `sqlite3_finalize` then waits on a connection mutex held by a Ractor that has stopped. I haven't reduced it to a minimal repro yet, so I don't know whether it belongs here or in Ruby. I'll follow up separately.

open.title: Proof of Concept: Release GVL in Statement#step
open.body:
Refs #287, but **I don't think this is ready to merge**. As described below the performance impact is very significant. I think this is something the library _should_ do, but it's a penalty that's hard to just eat.

This allows other threads to execute Ruby code (including performing more work sqlite operations if on another DB connection). This should significantly improve multithreaded performance, however as @tenderlove correctly predicted in #287 adds significant overhead to single-threaded performance.

This required wrapping all callbacks which can happen within statement execution with rb_thread_call_with_gvl.

I've written two benchmarks, one which shows why this could be a good idea and one which shows why it's a bad idea. It's unfortunately not clear cut.

### The good

https://gist.github.com/jhawthorn/ae84ee2723ff4930344778cfe40205a2

I made a benchmark based on making sqlite actually do work (a poorly optimized query) before returning, and then having multiple threads perform the same operation. This shows a very significant speed up as we are actually able to run the sqlite operations in parallel.

main

```
$ bundle exec ruby test.rb
single threaded:
0.9432485040742904
multi threaded:
1.1921860249713063
```

This branch:

```
$ bundle exec ruby test.rb
single threaded:
0.927121008047834
multi threaded:
0.17125224182382226
```

### The bad

https://gist.github.com/jhawthorn/492b6a9c5fb6bebe1ebfe985f52495de

When running a completely trivial query in a single thread, this is about 60% slower due to the need to release and re-acquire the GVL on every call to `Statement#step`. I don't think there's an easy way around this as even if our API was a more "bulk" operation (ie "return all rows" rather than "return one row") I believe we'll need the GVL every time we want to allocate a Ruby string and our memory buffer returned from SQLite is only good until our next call to `sqlite3_step`.

```
Comparison:
SELECT * LIMIT 1000 (gvl):     4336.3 i/s
SELECT * LIMIT 1000 (nogvl):     2705.2 i/s - 1.60x  slower
```

I do think this is capturing the absolute worst case as the query is completely trivial and doesn't even make allocations other than the one array per-row.

So that's where we're at. There might be some sort of compromise we could do like making the GVL releasing optional or based on a heuristic. I haven't yet investigated any way to make this faster, but it does seem unlikely we'll find a way to do this without a performance penalty.

### TODO

* [ ] execute_batch2 doesn't yet release the GVL (which probably makes it crashy if any callbacks exist)
* [ ] prepare and some other operations should likely also release the GVL
* [ ] It might be good to provide a UBF to `rb_thread_call_without_gvl`

open.title: Implement progress handler interface
open.body:
This adds support for the [`progress_handler`](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/progress_handler.html) SQLite interface. Such a callback is useful as it allows for statement timeouts to be defined. For example, we could define a `statement_timeout=` method on the database instance like so:
```ruby
def statement_timeout=( milliseconds )
  timeout_seconds = milliseconds.fdiv(1000)

  progress_handler do
    now = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    if @statement_timeout_deadline.nil?
      @statement_timeout_deadline = now + timeout_seconds
    elsif now > @statement_timeout_deadline
      next false
    else
      true
    end
  end
end
```

Note: I don't know C, so this PR was written using pattern matching (primarily on the `rb_sqlite3_busy_handler` and `busy_handler` methods), some Googling (for how to get the correct format for `rb_scan_args`), and ChatGPT (to explain what all of this C code was doing).

See https://github.com/sparklemotion/sqlite3-ruby/issues/299 .
